claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is a refractory high-entropy alloy that can be represented by the equiatomic Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 composition.
Thermal activation causes local elemental segregation in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local elemental segregation produces spatial variations in lattice parameters.
Regions with different lattice parameters develop mismatched thermal expansion.
Internal thermal-expansion mismatch generates internal stresses in HfNbTaTiZr.
Mismatch-generated internal stresses govern anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior from room temperature to 1250 °C.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr contains inherent compositional fluctuations and microstructural heterogeneity.
High-entropy alloys can contain nanoprecipitates and ordered or disordered solid-solution phases, making incipient phase differentiation broadly plausible.
Rapid quenching maintains a homogenized HfNbTaTiZr microstructure and suppresses segregation.
Aging at 600–800 °C promotes local elemental segregation and short-range ordering in HfNbTaTiZr.
The aged samples will have greater segregation and thermal-expansion mismatch than the quenched baseline.
Segregation-induced internal stresses increase cold-rolling hardening and microhardness.
Segregation-induced internal stresses can enhance tensile creep resistance at high temperature.
Segregation-induced internal stresses produce a more pronounced nonlinear temperature dependence of the elastic moduli.
Homogenized quenched samples have lower residual stresses and more ideal elastic and creep responses than aged samples.
The proposed comparison uses identically tested quenched and aged samples, with microscopy and diffraction used to quantify segregation and lattice-parameter variation.
The cited earlier studies provide trends supporting the proposed thermal-expansion-mismatch mechanism.
A lack of statistically significant response differences, or a lack of correlation between response differences and measured mismatch, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The upper temperature boundary for elastic-modulus testing is inconsistent: the design describes evaluation up to 1250 °C, whereas the measurement list specifies only 293–1100 K, whose upper bound is approximately 827 °C.
